prompt.context: Our client, SunFury, is a publicly traded solar developer and the largest builder of utility scale solar projects across the US. They have experienced incredible growth over the last 6 years, due largely to the rapidly falling solar module prices from China and the consistent US tax credit for solar projects. In 2017 the Solar Investment Tax Credit (ITC) will drop from 30% for all solar to 10% for utility and 0% for residential, forcing the industry to compete more closely with cheap coal and natural gas. It is August 2015, and SunFury has decided to expand their operations into the residential arena to better capture the ITC while it still exists.
prompt.question: SunFury has asked us to (1) estimate the potential value at stake, and (2) determine whether they should go ahead with their residential launch in 2016.

clarifying_info.q: Can we build solar everywhere in the US?
clarifying_info.a: See Handout 1 (solar radiation map). Expert analysis shows residential solar with SunFury panels is profitable when kWh/m2/day is >5 on an annualized basis.

clarifying_info.q: What is the population density by region?
clarifying_info.a: See Handout 2 (US population density map). Based on the two handouts, the population living in solar radiation zones >5 kWh/m2/day is between 30-50% (CA+TX alone is ~80M people).

clarifying_info.q: How many homes already have solar?
clarifying_info.a: You can assume 20-50%; the interviewer will provide 40% once you raise the question.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the average American home?
clarifying_info.a: The average American home is single story and roughly 1,600 sq ft (40 ft x 40 ft).

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of a SunFury solar panel?
clarifying_info.a: Each solar panel is 2m x 3m (approximately 6 ft x 9 ft).

exhibits.title: US Solar Radiation Map (Handout 1)
exhibits.shows: A map of the contiguous United States showing annualized solar radiation levels (kWh/m2/day) by region, sourced from NREL 1961-1990 data.
exhibits.data: Regions are shaded by solar radiation intensity; a footnote states residential solar is profitable when kWh/m2/day >5 on an annualized basis.

exhibits.title: US Population Density Map (Handout 2)
exhibits.shows: A map of the contiguous United States showing population density by region, sourced from the US Census Bureau.
exhibits.data: Population density varies significantly by region; high-density areas are concentrated in coastal and urban zones.

framework: Market sizing: estimate total addressable market (number of targetable homes and panels)
Competitive landscape: assess number of players, intensity of competition, and likely market share
Financial analysis: model revenues, costs, and profitability under the current ITC (30%) and post-2017 ITC (0% for residential)
Strategic fit: evaluate whether residential aligns with SunFury's existing utility-scale capabilities and timeline
Recommendation: decide whether to enter residential or double down on utility projects before ITC changes

questions.prompt: How many homes in the US can SunFury target for residential solar?
questions.guidance: Strong answer: Start with US population (320M), derive ~80-100M families, apply 40-80% single/multi-family home rate to get 32-80M homes, then narrow to solar-viable regions (30-50% of population in >5 kWh/m2/day zones), yielding 9.5-40M potential addressable homes. Then ask how many already have solar (provide 40%), arriving at a TAM of ~9M homes. Interviewer provides 9M if candidate gets stuck.

math.setup: US population → families → homes in viable solar zones → subtract existing solar adopters
steps: Apply ~36% in high-solar zones (30-50% range, use ~36% midpoint or use CA+TX logic) ≈ 15M potential homes (interviewer gives 15M after math)

questions.prompt: Given 9M targetable homes, how many solar panels could SunFury potentially sell?
questions.guidance: Strong answer: Determine panels per roof by dividing roof area by panel area, recognizing panels cannot overhang the roof edge. Great candidates use row x column logic: 40 ft wide ÷ 6 ft/panel = 6 panels wide; 40 ft tall ÷ 9 ft/panel = 4 panels tall; 6×4=24 panels (round to 25). Multiply by 9M homes.

math.setup: Roof dimensions → panels that fit per roof (row x column) → total panels across TAM
steps: Average roof: 1,600 sq ft = 40 ft × 40 ft
Panel size: 2m × 3m ≈ 6 ft × 9 ft = 54 sq ft
Simple area division: 1,600 / 54 ≈ 29 panels (but panels cannot overhang edges)
Row x column: 40 ft / 6 ft = 6 panels wide; 40 ft / 9 ft = 4 panels tall; 6 × 4 = 24 panels (round to 25)

questions.prompt: What information do you still need to recommend that SunFury move into residential solar?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a framework covering: (1) Revenue: price per panel / system, expected market share given fierce competition; (2) Costs: startup/capex, installation, marketing, operations; (3) Profitability: factor in 30% ITC available now vs. 0% post-2017; (4) Timeline: ITC drops in 2017, leaving only ~1 year from a 2016 launch; (5) Competition: many players competing, likely driving share well below 20%. Strong candidates recall the ITC timeline from the prompt without being prompted. Better candidates conclude that even upper-bound scenarios are unprofitable after ITC expires.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key risks and factors SunFury should weigh when deciding whether to enter the residential market?

categories.name: Regulatory / Tax
ideas: ITC drops from 30% to 0% for residential in 2017, leaving only ~1 year of subsidy after a 2016 launch
Utility ITC only drops to 10%, making utility projects relatively more attractive post-2017
Permitting complexity for residential installs varies by municipality

categories.name: Competitive Dynamics
ideas: Residential solar market is already crowded with many established players
Fierce competition likely drives available market share below 10-20%
SunFury has no residential brand recognition or installer network
Incumbents may engage in price wars to defend share

categories.name: Financial / Profitability
ideas: High startup costs (installer training, sales force, new systems) erode margins
Without ITC, residential solar cannot compete with cheap coal and natural gas
Short ITC window may not allow recovery of upfront investment
Opportunity cost: capital deployed in residential could instead lock in utility projects

categories.name: Operational / Capability Fit
ideas: SunFury's core competency is utility-scale; residential requires a very different go-to-market and service model
Need to build or acquire residential sales, installation, and maintenance capabilities
Customer acquisition cost in residential is high and fragmented

categories.name: Market / Demand
ideas: Large TAM (~9M homes) but realistic capturable share is small given competition
Saturation of early adopters; remaining market may be harder to convert
Geographic concentration in high-solar states (CA, TX) limits national reach

recommendation: SunFury should NOT enter the residential market at this time.

Instead, SunFury should focus resources on locking in and completing utility-scale projects before 2017, when the ITC for utility drops from 30% to 10% — still far more favorable than the 0% residential rate — protecting margins and leveraging existing core competencies.
risks: Fierce competition in residential will reduce SunFury's achievable market share to well below 20%
The ITC for residential goes to 0% in 2017, leaving only ~1 year from a 2016 launch — insufficient to recoup startup investment
High startup and customer acquisition costs make the residential business unprofitable even at optimistic market share assumptions
next_steps: Accelerate pipeline of utility-scale projects to maximize value captured before the utility ITC drops from 30% to 10% in 2017
Monitor residential market post-2017 to reassess entry if economics improve (e.g., further panel price declines, new incentives)
Evaluate whether any residential capabilities (e.g., installer partnerships) could be acquired cheaply as an option on future entry
